# Vortex dynamics

Lecture 11 · [Original notes](https://www.alucasphys.com/p7810s2026/p7810s2026_lecture11.pdf)

::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives"}
Derive vorticity transport, solve the viscously spreading point vortex, understand point vortex Hamiltonian dynamics and image vortices, and explain Kelvin's theorem and moving vortex filaments.
:::

## Taking the curl removes pressure {#sec-l11-vorticity}

For an incompressible fluid of constant density, define kinematic viscosity $\nu=\eta/\rho$ and vorticity $\boldsymbol\omega=\nabla\times\mathbf v$. The antisymmetric tensor $\omega_{ij}=\partial_iv_j-\partial_jv_i$ is the corresponding definition in arbitrary dimension. Navier–Stokes reads

$$
\partial_t\mathbf v+(\mathbf v\cdot\nabla)\mathbf v
=-\frac{\nabla P}{\rho}+\nu\nabla^2\mathbf v.
$$

Taking its curl eliminates the gradient of pressure. Using $\nabla\cdot\mathbf v=0$ and $\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\omega=0$ gives

$$
\partial_t\boldsymbol\omega+(\mathbf v\cdot\nabla)\boldsymbol\omega
=(\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\nabla)\mathbf v+\nu\nabla^2\boldsymbol\omega.
$$ {#eq-l11-vorticity}

The left side is transport with the fluid. The first term on the right stretches and tilts vortex lines: a material line element obeys the same inviscid stretching equation. The last term diffuses vorticity. For air, representative values are $\rho\sim1\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and $\nu\sim10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

In a strictly two dimensional flow, $v_z=0$ and $\partial_z=0$. The only vorticity component is $\omega=\omega_z$, so vortex stretching vanishes:

$$
\partial_t\omega+\mathbf v\cdot\nabla\omega=\nu\nabla^2\omega.
$$ {#eq-l11-2d}

An inviscid two dimensional vortex is carried along without changing its vorticity on each material element. This important simplification underlies both point vortex models and the distinctive behavior of two dimensional turbulence.

## A spreading point vortex {#sec-l11-diffusion}

A point vortex of circulation $\Gamma$ has $v_\theta=\Gamma/(2\pi r)$. Stokes's theorem gives $\int\omega\,d^2x=\Gamma$ through any disk containing its center, so its distributional vorticity is $\Gamma\delta^{(2)}(\mathbf x)$. With viscosity, rotational symmetry makes $\mathbf v\cdot\nabla\omega=0$. The diffusion Green function therefore solves the full vorticity equation:

$$
\omega(r,t)=\frac{\Gamma}{4\pi\nu t}
\exp\left(-\frac{r^2}{4\nu t}\right),\qquad t>0.
$$ {#eq-l11-gaussian}

The total circulation remains $\Gamma$ while its core broadens as $\sqrt{\nu t}$. Recover velocity by integrating $\omega=r^{-1}\partial_r(rv_\theta)$ and requiring regularity at $r=0$:

$$
v_\theta(r,t)=\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}
\left[1-e^{-r^2/(4\nu t)}\right].
$$ {#eq-l11-oseen}

At small radius the velocity is proportional to $r$, so the core rotates approximately as a solid body. At radii much larger than the core it retains the original $1/r$ velocity. Thus local vorticity spreads without immediately erasing the entire large scale circulation.

Radial force balance gives $\partial_rP=\rho v_\theta^2/r$, and hence

$$
P_\infty-P(r)=\rho\int_r^\infty\frac{v_\theta(r')^2}{r'}\,dr'.
$$ {#eq-l11-pressure}

**Supplemental derivation: central pressure.** Insert @eq-l11-oseen, use $a=4\nu t$, and set $s=r^2/a$. The required integral is

$$
\int_0^\infty\frac{(1-e^{-r^2/a})^2}{r^3}\,dr
=\frac{1}{2a}\int_0^\infty\frac{(1-e^{-s})^2}{s^2}\,ds
=\frac{\log2}{a}.
$$

The last equality follows by integration by parts, then integrating $(e^{-s}-e^{-2s})/s$. Consequently

$$
P_\infty-P(0)=\frac{\rho\Gamma^2\log2}{16\pi^2\nu t}.
$$

This is a model estimate, not a detailed tornado model. A vortex with characteristic speed $v_0$ at its core edge has a pressure deficit of order $\rho v_0^2$; $v_0\sim50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in air gives a few kilopascals.

## Interacting point vortices and Hamiltonian structure {#sec-l11-point}

Neglect viscosity and keep well separated cores. Each vortex moves with the velocity generated by the others:

$$
\dot{\mathbf r}_a=\sum_{b\ne a}\frac{\Gamma_b}{2\pi}
\frac{\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\mathbf r_a-\mathbf r_b)}{|\mathbf r_a-\mathbf r_b|^2}.
$$ {#eq-l11-point-motion}

The self field is excluded. Two equal circulations rotate about their midpoint; opposite equal circulations form a translating dipole. Their separation stays constant in this idealization.

These equations are Hamiltonian, although the two coordinates of a vortex play the role usually assigned to a position and momentum. A convention without double counting is

$$
\{x_a,y_b\}=\frac{\delta_{ab}}{\Gamma_a},\qquad
H=-\sum_{a<b}\frac{\Gamma_a\Gamma_b}{2\pi}\log\frac{|\mathbf r_a-\mathbf r_b|}{\ell_*}.
$$ {#eq-l11-hamiltonian}

The arbitrary length $\ell_*$ changes only an additive constant. For example,

$$
\dot x_a=\frac{1}{\Gamma_a}\frac{\partial H}{\partial y_a}
=-\sum_{b\ne a}\frac{\Gamma_b(y_a-y_b)}{2\pi|\mathbf r_a-\mathbf r_b|^2},
$$

which agrees with @eq-l11-point-motion. An action is $S=\int dt[\sum_a\Gamma_a y_a\dot x_a-H]$, up to total derivatives and equivalent symplectic conventions. Point vortex descriptions are useful for thin fluid layers and for effective motion of vortices in superfluids, with additional physics needed for core effects and dissipation.

**Supplemental derivation of the first order action.** Vary $S=\int dt[\Gamma y\dot x-H(x,y)]$ for one vortex with fixed endpoint variations. Variation of $y$ gives $\Gamma\dot x=\partial_yH$. Integrating the $\delta\dot x$ term by parts gives $-\Gamma\dot y=\partial_xH$. There is no independent quadratic kinetic term: after the fluid degrees of freedom are represented by ideal point vortices, their coordinates themselves carry the symplectic structure. The Hamiltonian here has been written in the conventional normalization for the vortex equations; multiplying both it and the symplectic coefficients by a common fluid density restores an energy normalization without changing the trajectories.

For two vortices, rotational symmetry conserves a circulation weighted angular impulse. For a vortex pair of opposite equal strengths, a center of circulation would involve division by zero, so the translating dipole must be understood directly from its induced velocities. This is a useful warning against treating point vortices exactly like massive particles with positive masses.

For a straight impermeable slip wall at $y=0$, a vortex $\Gamma$ at $(0,a)$ has an image $-\Gamma$ at $(0,-a)$. The two contributions cancel $v_y$ along the wall. The real vortex therefore travels parallel to the wall at speed $|\Gamma|/(4\pi a)$. This method enforces no penetration, not viscous no slip.

## Kelvin circulation and vortex filaments {#sec-l11-kelvin}

Let a closed material loop $C(t)$ move with the fluid. Differentiating its circulation requires differentiating both the velocity and the line element:

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\oint_{C(t)}\mathbf v\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell
=\oint_{C(t)}\left[D_t\mathbf v+\nabla(v^2/2)\right]\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell.
$$

For inviscid constant density flow, both terms are gradients. Their closed integrals vanish:

$$
\frac{d\Gamma_{C(t)}}{dt}=0.
$$ {#eq-l11-kelvin}

Conservative body forces can be included. A barotropic compressible fluid also admits a version using the specific enthalpy. Viscosity, baroclinic pressure forces, or singular changes of topology can invalidate this simple statement. Together with Stokes's theorem, Kelvin's result explains why an ideal vortex tube moves with the fluid.

In three dimensions, a thin vortex filament follows a curve $\mathbf r(s)$. The incompressible velocity induced by a filament of circulation $\Gamma$ is the Biot–Savart integral,

$$
\mathbf v(\mathbf x)=\frac{\Gamma}{4\pi}
\int\frac{d\mathbf r(s)\times[\mathbf x-\mathbf r(s)]}{|\mathbf x-\mathbf r(s)|^3}.
$$ {#eq-l11-biot-savart}

This follows from the same inverse curl problem as the magnetic field of a thin current. The filament is advected by its induced velocity plus any external flow, with a physical core regularizing the self field.

For a circular vortex ring of radius $R$, symmetry forces its self motion along the ring axis. The line integral has a logarithmic short distance divergence near the observation point. A core radius $a\ll R$ cuts it off, giving

$$
U_{\mathrm{ring}}\sim\frac{\Gamma}{4\pi R}\log\frac{R}{a}.
$$

A more precise constant inside the logarithm depends on the core model. The robust conclusions are axial propagation, speed proportional to circulation, and sensitivity to the slender core through a logarithm.

## Common pitfalls

Vorticity and velocity are different fields: nonzero azimuthal velocity need not imply nonzero local vorticity outside a core. Circulation conservation concerns a material loop. Images impose only the specified boundary condition. A filament's self velocity cannot be obtained by blindly evaluating a divergent ideal line integral.

## Exercises with solutions {#sec-l11-exercises}

1. **Vortex pair.** Two vortices $\Gamma$ are separated by $d$. Find their angular frequency.

   **Solution.** Each has speed $\Gamma/(2\pi d)$ and orbits at radius $d/2$, so $\Omega=\Gamma/(\pi d^2)$, with rotation direction set by the sign of $\Gamma$. For opposite signs both move at speed $|\Gamma|/(2\pi d)$ in the same direction.

2. **Core circulation.** What fraction of @eq-l11-gaussian lies inside radius $r$?

   **Solution.** Integrating $2\pi\int_0^r r'\omega\,dr'$ gives $\Gamma[1-e^{-r^2/(4\nu t)}]$. Half the circulation lies within $r=\sqrt{4\nu t\log2}$.

3. **Stretching.** An ideal narrow vortex tube doubles its length without changing volume. What happens to vorticity?

   **Solution.** Its cross section halves. Kelvin circulation fixes $\omega A$ for approximately uniform axial vorticity, so the vorticity doubles. This mechanism is absent in strictly two dimensional flow.
